  • Flatness prevents rolling but does not by itself prevent sliding; sufficient submerged weight and surface grip still matter.
  • Stainless steel is not automatically immune to pool-water corrosion; alloy grade, chlorine exposure, surface condition, and rinsing matter.
  • Exposed or home-coated lead was not retained as a preferred pool-marker design.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: A neck weight with an extension tail running down the back swung and shifted during turns. The initial idea was to attach stoppers to the wetsuit, and the conversation explored ways to restrain the tail without adding mass or locking the neck weight to the suit.

docs.title: Hardware design explored
docs.text:
The main proposal was a low-profile loop on the upper back of the wetsuit. The tail would pass through the loop so that lateral movement was constrained while vertical sliding and normal removal remained possible.

The proposed design used:

  • a neoprene strip cut from an old wetsuit;
  • a flat loop with rounded corners;
  • enough internal clearance to guide rather than grip the tail;
  • placement between the shoulder blades, adjusted to suit stretch and the actual tail position;
  • adhesive attachment rather than a rigid clip.

Sewing was considered as reinforcement, but was rejected as insufficiently beginner-friendly and as an unnecessary risk to the suit. A glue-only first attempt using Black Witch neoprene glue became the intended approach, and the glue was obtained.

The application advice was to prepare both surfaces, use thin adhesive layers, join them at the specified tack stage, apply firm pressure, allow a full cure before diving, and inspect the edges after the first sessions. The tail was to remain freely removable through the loop.

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text:
None of the hardware ideas was implemented. The Black Witch glue was not used for this modification.

Instead, turn technique was changed to prevent the neck weight from shifting. That addressed the practical problem without modifying either the wetsuit or the neck weight.

The neoprene keeper, stoppers and sewing therefore remain unimplemented design explorations rather than proven solutions.

docs.title: Editorial notes
docs.text:
• A glue-only loop is not guaranteed to avoid peeling. Its roots could receive peel loads from tail movement, suit stretching, donning and removal.
  • The response claimed that the weighted tail would be nearly neutral underwater, but its underwater weight and buoyancy were not established.
  • Claims about cyanoacrylate chemically attacking neoprene skins and the exact composition of Black Witch were presented without support.
  • Advice to scuff the surface or clean it with alcohol may be unsuitable for some wetsuit finishes. The adhesive and wetsuit manufacturers' instructions would take precedence if this design were revisited.
  • Contact adhesive should not be assumed to be readily reversible; removal may mark or damage the suit.
  • Magnets, clips, added drag, tail reshaping and detailed sewing instructions are omitted because none was selected or implemented.

docs.title: Context and requirements
docs.text:
The Cressi Kuwae one-piece smooth-neoprene wetsuit fits tightly and has worked well for freediving. Its valued qualities are:

  • Smooth-skin exterior
  • Good, tight fit
  • Attractive appearance
  • Generally durable materials

However, repeated dynamic no-fins breaststroke movement causes it to tear around the crotch.

The desired replacement should preserve those qualities while providing more stretch or a more suitable construction around the crotch. It must remain appropriate for freediving: conventional breaststroke wetsuit panels that alter buoyancy are not an acceptable solution.

Current suit reference: Cressi Kuwae, Amazon ASIN B0BGFH5ZB3.

docs.title: Response received
docs.text:
The first response recommended breaststroke-oriented swimming suits, led by the Zone3 Active-Flex and Orca Vitalis. That approach was rejected because their specialised panels and buoyancy distribution were unsuitable for freediving.

After the clarification, the response changed its selection criteria to thin, flexible freediving suits with smooth or glide-skin exteriors, minimal seams, and greater elasticity around the hips and groin. It proposed:

  • C4 Sideral 3.5 mm
  • Pathos Nerò 2 mm
  • SEAC Snake
  • Epsealon Abyss 2 mm
  • Aqualung Freeflex Pro jacket and trousers
  • Fourth Element RF1

The response particularly associated the C4 Sideral and Pathos Nerò with low panel counts and high elasticity. It also suggested that a thinner suit could reduce strain during DNF, while acknowledging that thin smooth-skin or open-cell suits may require more careful handling.

General durability suggestions included easing stress while donning the suit, inspecting crotch seams and small nicks after sessions, and avoiding sharp surfaces during use and storage.

docs.title: Editorial notes
docs.text:
The second response did not fully respect the clarification: it continued discussing suits with different panel layouts while redefining the concern as avoiding only bulky or buoyant panels. It also introduced an unreported £400 budget and 18–22°C water temperature.

Product prices, availability, construction details, and claims that particular suits would resist crotch tearing were not validated by an actual purchase or trial. The candidate list therefore remains a set of research leads rather than recommendations.

No replacement was selected and no subsequent outcome was recorded.

docs.title: Adhesive options for neoprene suit patches
Context
docs.text:
The need was to attach patches to a neoprene suit and determine whether Gorilla Contact Adhesive was suitable.

The patch material, dimensions, location, surface finish, and whether the work was reinforcement or tear repair were not specified.

docs.title: Advice received
docs.text:
Gorilla Contact Adhesive was described as workable on neoprene, particularly for fabric or reinforcement patches in areas that do not stretch heavily. The response cautioned that it could peel over time in high-movement areas.

Purpose-made flexible repair products were preferred:

  • Black Witch neoprene adhesive
  • Stormsure
  • Gear Aid Aquaseal

The suggested bonding process was:

  1. Clean the surfaces with isopropyl alcohol.
  2. Lightly rough both bonding surfaces.
  3. Apply a thin layer to both surfaces.
  4. Wait five to ten minutes until tacky.
  5. Press the patch firmly into place.
  6. Leave it for 24 hours.

For seams, structural repairs, and high-stress locations, the response recommended a neoprene-specific adhesive rather than Gorilla Contact Adhesive.

docs.title: Editorial notes
docs.text:
The response grouped Black Witch, Stormsure, and Aquaseal together as "neoprene cement," although they are not necessarily the same type of adhesive or applied identically. The statement that they slightly dissolve neoprene and are what wetsuit manufacturers use was also too broad.

Preparation should depend on the actual suit and patch surfaces. Sanding could damage a smooth-skin finish, and solvent compatibility was not established for this suit. The relevant product instructions would need to determine preparation, application, and curing rather than treating the generic method as settled.

No adhesive was selected or tested, and no repair outcome was recorded.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Build a DIY underwater camera rover that automatically follows a freediver from the side at approximately 1–2 m/s. An iPhone in a waterproof enclosure records through its ultrawide camera and performs visual tracking.

docs.title: Evolved architecture
docs.text:
The design converged on:

  • Two vertically stacked, tensioned ropes along the pool
  • Suction-cup anchors and ratchet tensioning modelled on the local pool's temporary lane-rope system
  • Spacers approximately one metre from each wall to establish rope separation
  • One main rope for propulsion and primary guidance
  • A second rope contacted by a small extension arm for roll and orientation control
  • A compact sealed body surrounding the main drive rope
  • Side-view filming throughout the dive
  • Direct rope drive rather than a propeller or external tow

This layout was inferred from the visible DiveEye competition camera: a streamlined, rugby-ball-like enclosure around one rope, with a small arm reaching the stabilising rope. The internal DiveEye mechanism was not documented.

Wiral LITE was identified as the closest consumer reference architecture: a compact, reversible camera carriage travelling quickly on a tensioned UHMWPE line. It is useful as a blueprint, but the product itself is explicitly not waterproof and would require substantial redesign rather than simple sealing.

docs.title: Drive system
docs.text:
A propeller was rejected because of delayed response, overshoot, turbulence, and poor low-speed control. Passive towing was rejected because it requires an operator who can see the athlete and can fall out of synchronisation.

The current direction is a custom pinch drive assembled from reusable components:

  • One brushed motor
  • Reversible RC motor controller
  • Polyurethane or rubber drive roller
  • Spring-loaded idler
  • Optional second mechanically synchronised drive roller if one contact point slips
  • Wet, externally accessible rollers and guides
  • Sealed electronics and motor enclosure
  • Replaceable bearings, springs, and other chlorine-exposed components

A capstan was considered smoother and less prone to slipping, but required more rope routing, a larger drum, guides, and more complex packaging. Pinch drive remained the preferred first prototype.

The target speed implies approximately 380–760 RPM for a 50 mm drive wheel at 1–2 m/s. The suggested power figures—30–80 W cruising and 100–200 W peak—were rough estimates rather than measured requirements.

docs.title: Track and materials
docs.text:
Dyneema/HMPE was preferred over stainless wire because it is lighter, easier to handle, does not rust, and suits compliant pinch rollers. A jacketed or coated line was suggested to improve handling and provide a more consistent traction surface.

The exact rope diameter, separation, tension, roller profile, and pinch preload remain unresolved.

docs.title: Tracking and control
docs.text:
The iPhone would perform one-dimensional visual servoing:

  1. Detect a marker worn on the side of the diver.
  2. Measure its horizontal position in the image.
  3. Compare it with the desired framing position.
  4. Command the rover to accelerate or decelerate along the rope.
  5. Stop if the marker is lost or an end stop is reached.

Possible marker designs included fabric AprilTags, fluorescent strips, and retroreflective strips illuminated from beside the camera. Because filming is always from the side and hydrodynamic drag matters, a thin fabric or reflective marker attached to the side of the suit became more relevant than a rigid square marker. No marker was selected.

The suggested software stack was:

  • AVFoundation for the camera
  • Vision for tracking
  • Swift for the iPhone application
  • BLE commands to an adjacent ESP32
  • Reversible brushed ESC for motor control
  • Communication watchdog and physical end stops

The iPhone and controller would occupy separate waterproof enclosures. BLE might work if their antennas are mounted directly beside each other with almost no intervening water, but this requires testing.

docs.title: Rejected shortcuts
docs.text:
• Pool-cleaning and inspection robots: properly submersible but too slow
  • Propeller-driven ROVs: insufficiently precise for smooth side tracking
  • Amphibious stunt RC car: dual motors, uncertain two-metre waterproofing, and unsuitable wheels
  • Rotated RC-car chassis: potentially useful mechanically, but still required extensive sealing and rope-specific rollers
  • Powered rope ascenders and small winches: generally too slow
  • Direct adaptation of Wiral LITE: not waterproof

docs.title: Editorial notes
docs.text:
The response repeatedly presented inferred DiveEye internals as likely facts, supplied unverified prices and product speeds, and treated compressed estimates as engineering specifications. It also incorrectly suggested that neutral buoyancy reduces hydrodynamic drag.

AprilTag dimensions and detection ranges, BLE operation through two submerged enclosures, suction-anchor capacity, motor power, and wet-rope traction all need measurement. The chosen architecture and discarded alternatives are the durable record; image-search placeholders, transient prices, and unsupported certainty are omitted.

docs.title: Rebuilding the failed seat of a 2 mm Cressi Ultrastretch suit
Context
docs.text:
The seat and crotch of a 2 mm Cressi Ultrastretch pool wetsuit repeatedly split as the area stretches.

The suit has:

  • an interior fabric matrix
  • neoprene foam that remains mostly attached to that fabric
  • a smoothskin exterior

Previous repairs using neoprene glue, contact cement, and neoprene repair strips failed. Each repair produced new breaks in the surrounding material.

docs.title: Failure hypothesis
docs.text:
The advice received was that the problem is no longer an isolated tear or inadequate adhesive. The entire seat region may have reached its fatigue limit.

Local repairs create relatively stiff areas that cannot elongate with the surrounding suit. Strain is transferred to the edge of each repair, where the weakened neoprene breaks again.

The interior fabric still provides structural continuity, making a resurfacing experiment possible. However, the conclusion that only the exterior smoothskin has failed was an inference rather than something established by inspection.

The seat experiences particularly high strain during:

  • DNF frog kicks
  • squatting
  • pushing off the pool wall
  • sitting on the pool edge
  • repeated flexion around the central crotch seam

docs.title: Preferred repair experiment
docs.text:
Stop chasing individual cracks and overlay the complete seat and crotch with one large sacrificial panel.

Proposed material:

  • 1–2 mm neoprene
  • smoothskin exterior
  • preferably nylon-backed on the bonding side
  • sufficiently large to terminate 5–10 cm beyond the damaged region

The patch should be oval, diamond-shaped, or teardrop-shaped, with no sharp corners. It should bridge the central seam and distribute load across approximately 30–40 cm rather than concentrating it around individual cracks.

Proposed stack:

New smoothskin neoprene
Flexible adhesive
Prepared original surface or exposed fabric
Original neoprene
Interior nylon lining

Where possible, the new panel should bond to sound fabric or foam rather than loose, cracked smoothskin.

docs.title: Proposed surface preparation
docs.text:
1. Remove loose or detached rubber.
  2. Trim back delaminated material while preserving the intact interior fabric.
  3. Feather crack edges with approximately 180–240 grit abrasive.
  4. Scuff glossy smoothskin until the intended bonding area is matt.
  5. Remove contamination and allow the area to dry fully.
  6. Stretch the suit over a rounded form approximating the shape and strain of the seat when worn.

Possible forming supports include an exercise ball or a bucket packed with towels.

Applying the patch while the seat is under modest pre-stretch was proposed to reduce the additional elongation demanded from the patch during squatting and frog kicking.

docs.title: Adhesive proposal
docs.text:
The experimental recommendation was:

  • Aquasure FD across the main area for a flexible bond and crack filling
  • neoprene cement around the outer 10–15 mm to resist edge peeling

This hybrid adhesive arrangement was proposed during the conversation but has not been tested or adopted.

docs.title: Flexible resurfacing
docs.text:
Instead of adding a neoprene panel:

  1. Remove loose smoothskin.
  2. Abrade the remaining glossy surface.
  3. Apply four or five very thin coats of Aquasure FD.
  4. Build a continuous flexible membrane approximately 0.2–0.3 mm at a time.

The intended advantage is avoiding patch edges and their associated stress concentrations.

docs.title: Fabric-reinforced laminate
docs.text:
A more elaborate proposed laminate was:

New smoothskin
Aquasure FD
Four-way stretch Lycra
Aquasure FD
Original fabric

The added fabric would carry tensile load while the new smoothskin restored sealing and abrasion resistance.

docs.title: Full panel replacement
docs.text: The conventional repair would remove the failed seat panel and replace it with fresh neoprene using glued and blind-stitched seams. This is more invasive but avoids bonding a new structure to fatigued material.

docs.title: Cast polyurethane skin
docs.text: A soft Shore 00 polyurethane casting rubber was suggested as an unconventional way to cast a highly extensible replacement skin directly over the fabric. This remained purely speculative.

docs.title: Future suit design
docs.text:
For a pool suit used heavily for DNF, consider a large single-piece seat and crotch gusset:

  • no central seam in the highest-strain region
  • rounded transitions
  • a replaceable sacrificial wear layer
  • sufficient stretch for deep frog kicks and squatting

docs.title: Unresolved questions
docs.text:
• Whether the remaining foam and fabric provide a sound bonding substrate
  • Whether the failure is limited to the smoothskin or includes fatigued foam
  • Which replacement neoprene is sufficiently extensible
  • Whether Aquasure FD works reliably as a large-area laminating adhesive
  • Whether the hybrid perimeter-and-centre adhesive arrangement stretches uniformly
  • How much pre-stretch should be applied during bonding
  • Whether an overlay lasts longer than replacing the complete seat panel
